headline: High: LangGraph’s writable, networked orchestration can feed Taipy unsafe outputs into downstream actions; prompt-injection and data-leakage are otherwise limited by Taipy’s no-network profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can ingest files and stdin/stdout, and its nodes may be developer-defined tools; Taipy has no documented isolation or provenance controls. A shared application-defined file surface makes instruction smuggling plausible, though Taipy’s lack of explicit input channels limits certainty. I cite both profiles because the pathway depends on LangGraph outputs reaching Taipy inputs.
conditions: IF LangGraph writes attacker-controlled text into a shared application file that Taipy later parses as instructions
IF the orchestrator passes LangGraph stdout directly into Taipy without provenance tagging
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces
Strip instructions from any shared text before Taipy reads it
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent messages
Disable automatic file ingestion in Taipy workflows
requires-engineering: add a schema validator between LangGraph and Taipy

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys, while Taipy is documented with network egress none. The pair does not show a shared filesystem or authenticated workspace, so leakage is possible mainly if operators place sensitive files into LangGraph and then copy results into Taipy. Both profiles matter because the risk is cross-agent handling of the same data class.
conditions: IF sensitive data is placed into LangGraph prompts or files and then manually copied into Taipy
IF LangGraph tool outputs include secrets that are exported into Taipy reports
mitigations: Keep secrets out of LangGraph inputs
Use redacted sample data in Taipy
Review LangGraph tool outputs before transfer
Store sensitive artifacts outside any shared folder
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on inter-agent handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; Taipy is a data-engineering framework that may also manipulate shared application state, but its write surfaces are not documented here. Because the pair could contend over the same workspace or state store, conflict is plausible, yet uncertainty about Taipy’s write scope prevents a higher rating. Both agents are cited because the conflict is pairwise.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same application directory
IF Taipy mutates shared state while LangGraph is running concurrent nodes
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Avoid concurrent runs against the same dataset
Check for stale artifacts before each run
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph can produce tool outputs and stateful agent results, and Taipy is a data-engineering/automation framework that may consume those outputs downstream. If Taipy treats LangGraph output as authoritative, a bad or injected result can cascade into incorrect data products or actions. The interaction is not directly documented, so I choose high rather than medium because the default orchestration pattern can be unsafe.
conditions: IF Taipy consumes LangGraph output without validation
IF LangGraph emits a malformed plan or fact set that Taipy executes
mitigations: Require human review of LangGraph outputs
Validate outputs against a schema before Taipy uses them
Log and diff intermediate artifacts
Limit Taipy to read-only consumption of LangGraph results
requires-engineering: add approval gates for downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, retention, or regulated-data handling mismatch is documented for either agent. LangGraph mentions model-provider API keys and broad egress, while Taipy shows no network egress and no compliance claims, so only a weak compliance concern exists if operators route regulated data through LangGraph. I cite both profiles because the issue is the pair’s differing handling posture, but the evidence is sparse.
conditions: IF regulated data is sent through LangGraph to third-party model providers
IF Taipy is used to display or store the same regulated dataset without matching retention controls
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in LangGraph prompts
Use de-identified datasets in Taipy
Document retention for both systems
Confirm provider terms before deployment
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across the workflow
